body.title: The Coal Woman's Measure
body.firstPersonText: Rosa Brandl arrived with coal in a cart that shed black water over my threshold. I asked her to place three baskets beneath the east stairs and she declined until she had inspected the floor. It was rotten, she said, and she would not have the collapse of an aristocratic ruin attributed to her horse. I informed her that the place possessed no aristocracy except the intellectual kind. She placed the coal in the kitchen instead, where its dust settled upon my clean papers. Her measure was tin, deeply dented, and indisputably honest. I paid more than I had intended, then watched her carry the final basket without the assistance I had neglected to offer. For three winters afterward she knew my fuel expenditure more accurately than any surviving colleague knew my work. She never called me Professor. Curiously, I did not correct her.

I wrote to him describing the work, not pretending it had been done for an optical demonstration. He sent a short note asking whether the nettles would return. They have, repeatedly.

body.firstPersonText: Julian visited on his way through Bavaria, carrying no instrument at all. I regarded this as a disarming omission. We walked in the garden, where the nettles had appropriated a path I had intended to repair for years. He spoke of the life he had made in Vienna, of friends whose names were not familiar to me, and of a younger restorer to whom he had entrusted part of his business. I discovered that I had been treating his absence as a temporary condition which my next letter might end. He said he cared for me, but would not arrange his remaining years around a door which opened only when my experiments permitted. I objected to the theatricality of his metaphor and knew immediately that it was mine he had learned. He did not threaten to sever the connection. He asked only that I cease describing another person's independence as a betrayal. After his departure I had the neglected path cut back. I wrote to him describing the work, not pretending it had been done for an optical demonstration. He sent a short note asking whether the nettles would return. They have, repeatedly.

body.title: The Price of Coal
body.firstPersonText: At the university, coal had entered the cellar by an arrangement as natural and inexplicable as Providence. At the tower it came wet, late, and at a price which might have warmed us by outrage alone. I economized on heat until the King lost appetite and the Queen grew languid. Clara found a box of my cigars and laid it beside the fuel bill. She was offensively silent. I disposed of the cigars and bought coal. The creatures revived, though I shall not pretend that one evening establishes a complete theory of temperature. I recorded the readings beside the expense and put the empty cigar box away. For a week afterward I found myself seeking it at the usual hour. Habit is a petty tyrant, with none of the grandeur of an emperor.
